statement: The head of ICT risk at a mid-sized bank is setting the review calendar for the bank's ICT risk management framework. How often does DORA require the framework to be reviewed, and which events should trigger an extra review outside that regular cycle?

The founder of a small payment business operates under its country's exemption for small payment institutions instead of holding a full licence. The founder assumes that being exempt also keeps the business outside DORA. Is the business covered by DORA at all?

The operations manager of a crypto exchange that keeps its customers' tokens in custody is designing client reporting. How often must the exchange send each customer a statement of the crypto-assets it holds for them, and can customers also ask for one in between?

A crypto exchange based in Singapore, with no MiCA authorisation, has customers in Germany who signed up after finding the platform on their own. Can it keep serving them without an EU authorisation, and can it email them about the new tokens and services it is about to launch?

The compliance officer of a crypto exchange authorised under MiCA is setting up how the exchange handles outgoing transfers of crypto to other crypto exchanges. For each of these transfers, what information about the sender and about the recipient must accompany it?
gap_note: The information on the originator and the beneficiary that must accompany a transfer of crypto-assets is not set in DORA, MiCA or PSD2: it is in Regulation (EU) 2023/1113, outside the corpus. MiCA covers transfer services only through the client agreement (Article 82(1)) and ESMA guidelines (Article 82(2)).

statement: A mid-sized crypto exchange authorised under MiCA is drafting its business continuity policy. What must that policy contain under the crypto rules, in terms of both what it must aim to achieve and which ICT continuity and recovery plans it must include?
A consumer complained to her payment provider about a card payment that was charged twice. How long does the provider have to reply to her complaint, and in what situation may it take longer?

A consumer has only just noticed that, about six weeks ago, her gym collected a much larger monthly amount than usual by direct debit. She had signed the direct debit mandate, but the form did not state a fixed amount. Can she still get the money back from her bank even though she signed the mandate?

A bank's head of procurement is renegotiating the contract with the vendor that runs the bank's core banking platform. As part of that renegotiation, the head of procurement is looking at the bank's right to end the contract. In which situations must the bank be able to end its contract with the vendor?

The risk officer of a mid-sized insurance company is briefing the board on what happens if the company falls short of DORA. If the company's national supervisor fined it for falling short of DORA, what is the maximum fine the company could face?
gap_note: Assumed: the insurer's national competent authority, in any Member State (DORA Article 46(k)). In the corpus: DORA leaves administrative penalties to each Member State's law (Article 50(3)) and requires the power to impose measures of a pecuniary nature (Article 50(4)(c)), with no amount. Missing: the maximum fine itself, which national law sets. The only DORA figure, Article 35(8), caps periodic penalty payments on critical ICT third-party service providers.

statement: The security operations lead of a bank has detected a serious cyber threat aimed at the bank. No incident has happened, and no system or service has been affected. The lead assumes that, as with a major incident, DORA makes it mandatory for the bank to report this threat to its supervisor. Must the bank report the threat to its supervisor?

A bank has been required by its supervisor to carry out threat-led penetration testing under DORA. Rather than hiring an external testing firm, the bank wants its in-house red team to perform the tests. Can the bank use its own staff as the testers?

A software company provides an IT service to many financial firms. All of its clients operate only in the EU country where the company is based, and it provides the service only there. Because so many financial firms use the service, its managers assume the company could be designated under DORA as a critical IT provider subject to EU-level oversight. Can the company be designated as critical?

The head of cybersecurity at a mid-sized bank wants the bank to join a group of other financial firms that exchange information about cyber threats, such as indicators of compromise and attackers' tactics. Under what conditions does DORA allow the bank to share this kind of information with the other members of the group?

A cloud provider has just been designated under DORA as a critical IT provider for the EU financial sector. Its finance director is looking into the oversight fees that come with the designation. How much will the company have to pay in these fees each year?
gap_note: In the corpus: a critical ICT third-party service provider pays oversight fees that fully cover the Lead Overseer's necessary oversight expenditure and are proportionate to its turnover (DORA Article 43(1)), and the Commission fixes the amount and the way of payment by delegated act (Article 43(2)). Missing: the amount, how it is calculated and when it is paid, set in that delegated act (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1505), a Level 2 act outside the corpus. The figure for one provider also depends on its turnover, which the need does not state.

statement: The founders of a start-up plan to offer a new crypto-asset to the public in the EU. The token is not a stablecoin and is not a financial instrument. The founders assume that their national regulator must approve the token's white paper before they can launch the offer. Does the white paper need the regulator's approval before the offer goes ahead?

A retail investor holds tokens of a stablecoin whose value is tied to a basket made up of several currencies and gold. Is she entitled to have the issuer take back her tokens and pay her out at any time she chooses?

A tech start-up that holds no financial licence of any kind plans to issue its own stablecoin, pegged one-to-one to the euro, and to offer it to the public in the EU. Is the start-up allowed to issue this token as it stands today?

An employee of a crypto exchange learned at work, before any public announcement, that her employer would soon list a token already traded on other crypto platforms. Listings on her employer's platform usually make a token's price jump. Before the announcement, she bought some of the token for herself on another platform. Did that purchase break the EU rules against market abuse in crypto?

A consumer association is alarmed by a meme coin that is being aggressively marketed and sold to retail investors across the EU. The coin is a crypto token, not a stablecoin. Can ESMA, the EU securities markets authority, temporarily ban the marketing and sale of this coin throughout the EU?

The general counsel of an investment fund is reviewing a deal in which the fund plans to buy 25% of the shares of a crypto exchange that is authorised under MiCA. Does the fund have to notify the exchange's supervisor before it completes the purchase?

The compliance officer of a crypto exchange is reviewing the firm's licensing position. The exchange has served clients under its country's national crypto rules since before MiCA started to apply. It has applied for a MiCA authorisation and is still waiting for a decision. Until when may the exchange keep offering its services without that authorisation?

Two founders are setting up a business that will offer only money remittance, sending money abroad for its customers without opening payment accounts for them. They plan to apply for a payment institution licence. What is the minimum amount of capital the business must hold to get that licence?
gap_note: In the corpus: initial capital of at least EUR 20 000 at authorisation for a payment institution that provides only the payment service of point (6) of Annex I (PSD2 Article 7(a)), and the definition of money remittance (Article 4(22)). Missing: PSD2 Annex I, the list of payment services, which the corpus does not contain, so nothing in the corpus ties money remittance to point (6), and so to the EUR 20 000 tier rather than the EUR 125 000 tier of Article 7(c).

statement: A bank plans to raise the monthly fee it charges its consumer customers for their current accounts. The accounts are already open under the customers' existing contracts, and the bank wants the higher fee to apply to these accounts. How far in advance must the bank tell the customers before the higher fee takes effect?

A consumer sent a bank transfer and typed the payee's IBAN herself, but she got one digit wrong. Her bank carried out the transfer, and the money went to the wrong account, which belongs to a stranger. Is her bank responsible for getting her money back?

A consumer's bank card was stolen, and the thief used it to make purchases online. For those purchases her bank never asked for an extra verification step, such as a code sent to her phone, and she did nothing dishonest. She believes customers always bear the first 50 euros of losses from a stolen card. Does she have to bear any part of the loss herself?

The owner of a small online shop is looking into the fees the shop pays each time one of its customers pays by card. What is the maximum interchange fee that may be applied to consumer debit card payments in the EU?
gap_note: No node states a cap on interchange fees. In the corpus: PSD2 Article 62(4) only says that interchange fees are regulated under Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 and bars the payee from requesting charges for those payment instruments. Missing: the maximum interchange fee for consumer debit card transactions, in Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/751 (the Interchange Fee Regulation), outside the corpus.

statement: A consumer has just moved to another EU country. She asked two banks there for a basic current account, and both turned her down. Does EU law oblige a bank in her new country to open a basic current account for her?
gap_note: No node gives a consumer a right to open a payment account. In the corpus: PSD2 governs framework contracts once concluded, and gives payment institutions, not consumers, access to credit institutions' payment account services (Article 36). Missing: the right of access to a payment account with basic features and the grounds on which a bank may refuse it, in Directive 2014/92/EU (the Payment Accounts Directive) and the national law transposing it, outside the corpus.

statement: The head of IT at a licensed payment institution is dealing with a major ICT-related incident that the firm has suffered. Under DORA, which authority must receive the firm's report on this incident: the same authority that granted the firm its payment institution licence, or a different one?

A fintech runs an app that, with each user's permission, collects the balances and transactions of the user's accounts at several banks and shows them in one place. The fintech never holds or moves users' money and is registered with its national supervisor. Its founders assume DORA applies only to banks and licensed payment firms. Does DORA apply to the fintech?
